messages.author: b8863e2cc3f8818f
messages.subject: Hierarchical Model: Convergence Problem
parts:
Dear all,

I wonder whether you can help me to find a solution for the convergence problem of the attached hierarchical model using a simple simulated data set. The data aims to simulate allele counts of rare and common genetic variants and its effects on blood pressure.

Using the IWLS-EM algorithm of the R/BhGLM package [1], the model converges easily with correct results with less than 4 iterations and less than 1 second run-time (results not shown). However, the NUTS algorithm of the R/STAN (V2.4.0) package strongly overestimates the parameters with two chains and 10,000 iterations running for 20 hours. I have attached the R/STAN script and output (for 1000 iterations, about 2 hours).

My understanding is, that just adding more iterations won't solve the problem, but the HMC/NUTS algorithm has to be configured/tuned for this problem. I was actually expecting much better performance of the HMC/NUTS sampler for hierarchical models with highly correlated parameters.

Any help is much appreciated!

Best regards and a happy New Year!

Will

References:
[1] http://www.ssg.uab.edu/bhglm/files/BhGLM_1.1.0.zip

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical Model: Convergence Problem
parts:
You're right --- more iterations won't help.

There will be a convergence problem due to the
multiplicative non-identifiability of gamma and alpha.
if you multiply gamma[1] by C and divide alpha[1] by C,
you get the same linear predictor.

The Cauchy priors aren't strong enough to pin down the
values.

As you can see in your output, the posterior 95%
intervals are very wide for the parameters.

This is usually bad news. There's a chapter in the
manual on problematic posteriors.

I don't see what the gamma are giving you here as only
the product of gamma and alpha is identified in the likelihood.

- Bob

messages.author: b8863e2cc3f8818f
messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical Model: Convergence Problem
parts:
Dear Bob,

thanks for your advice! The idea of this model is to separate effects of individual genetic variants and grouped genetic variants, especially to increase the power of detecting effects of rare variants with sparse data, similar to testing a genetic risk score  (see Paper PMID 22144906). Your arguments why this model is not well-identified sound convincing, however, I wonder why this model can be easily fitted with the R/BHGLM (IWLS-EM algorithm) package which uses a very similar setup (although the prior variances are constructed as hierarchical (half)Cauchy distributions, which shared hyperparameters per group), so my impression was that it has to do something with the algorithm.

Apart from convergence problems with STAN, my simulations (with the R/BGHLM package) show that when using weakly informative priors (Cauchy(0,1)), the fraction of Bayesian p values with p < 0.05 is considerably higher, which  in my opinion indicates an overfitting problem because the group effect and the variant effects are estimated from the same data.

Do you also see a problem there?

Best, Will

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Hierarchical Model: Convergence Problem
parts:
> On Jan 5, 2015, at 4:13 AM, Wilmar Igl <wilma...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Bob,
>
> thanks for your advice! The idea of this model is to separate effects of individual genetic variants and grouped genetic variants, especially to increase the power of detecting effects of rare variants with sparse data, similar to testing a genetic risk score (see Paper PMID 22144906). Your arguments why this model is not well-identified sound convincing, however, I wonder why this model can be easily fitted with the R/BHGLM (IWLS-EM algorithm) package which uses a very similar setup (although the prior variances are constructed as hierarchical (half)Cauchy distributions, which shared hyperparameters per group), so my impression was that it has to do something with the algorithm.

I don't know BHGLM, and its home page only provides a zip, no indication
of what the algorithm is. But IWLS-EM sounds like an optimization algorithm,
not an MCMC sampler. Because there are priors, there's a well-defined
maximum likelihood set of parameters. And optimization is much much faster
than MCMC in general.

You can try Stan's optimizer and see what happens. Usually you can't
optimize a hierarchical model, so maybe BHGLM is doing something more
like marginal maximum likelihood, since it claims to be handling hierarchical
models. There you usually maximize one set of params while marginalizing
out the other, then use the data again to fit the other set of parameters
conditioned on the max of the first:

target: p(alpha,beta|data)

alpha* = ARGMAX_alpha INTEGRAL p(alpha,beta|data) d.beta

beta* = ARGMAX p(beta|alpha,data)

But a posterior mode isn't the same as a Bayesian posterior mean.
And an MML solution is a different thing again.

> Apart from convergence problems with STAN, my simulations (with the R/BGHLM package) show that when using weakly informative priors (Cauchy(0,1)), the fraction of Bayesian p values with p < 0.05 is considerably higher,

> which in my opinion indicates an overfitting problem because the group effect and the variant effects are estimated from the same data.
>
> Do you also see a problem there?

Stan doesn't use the data twice.

In full Bayesian inference (as opposed to, say maximum
penalized likelihood or maximum marginal likelihood), you only
use the data once to fit the entire model.

- Bob
